title: Highest-Protein Fish: Ranking Per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Fish per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: A clear ranking of cooked fish by protein per 100 grams, including tuna, mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon, with serving-size and calorie context.
seo.search_intent: Informational: compare commonly eaten fish by protein using a consistent cooked state and understand how calories, fat and serving size change the practical picture.

excerpt: Among the cooked fish compared, yellowfin tuna provides about 29.2 g of protein per 100 g. Mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon are mostly in the 22–24 g range, so a normal serving of any of them can provide a substantial amount of protein.
content_html:
Fish is one of the most protein-dense food groups. For many species, a typical 5-ounce serving can provide roughly 30–40 grams of protein.

To keep the comparison easy to read, the main table uses cooked fish. Raw fish, oil-packed canned fish, salted fish and cooked fillets can differ in water, sodium and fat, so mixing them in one ranking can make preparation look like a species difference.

Cooked fish ranked by protein

FishProtein per 100 gApprox. calories
Yellowfin tuna29.2 g130 kcal
Atlantic mackerel23.9 g262 kcal
Farmed rainbow trout23.8 g168 kcal
Swordfish23.5 g172 kcal
Wild rainbow trout22.9 g150 kcal
Atlantic cod22.8 g105 kcal
Farmed Atlantic salmon22.1 g206 kcal
Haddock20.0 g90 kcal

The gap between the first fish and most of the rest is noticeable: the tuna entry provides about 29.2 g/100 g, compared with 22.8 g for cod and 22.1 g for salmon. By contrast, mackerel, farmed trout and swordfish are separated by less than half a gram per 100 g, so normal serving-size variation can matter more than that small difference.

1. Tuna: about 29 grams of protein per 100 g

Cooked yellowfin tuna provides about 29.2 g of protein per 100 g for roughly 130 calories. In the USDA entry used here, fat is very low at about 0.6 g/100 g.

A 5-ounce cooked portion therefore provides roughly 41 g of protein.

Protein is not the only factor to consider with tuna. Mercury varies by species. FDA/EPA place canned light tuna among their “Best Choices,” albacore/white tuna in a higher-mercury category, and bigeye tuna among the “Choices to Avoid” for people who are or may become pregnant, those who are breastfeeding, and children. The distinction matters because “tuna” is not one nutritionally or toxicologically uniform food.

2. Mackerel: nearly 24 g of protein, but much more energy than cod

Cooked Atlantic mackerel provides about 23.9 g of protein per 100 g, almost identical to farmed rainbow trout at 23.8 g.

The calorie difference is much larger. Atlantic mackerel in this comparison provides about 262 kcal/100 g, versus 168 kcal for the trout and 105 kcal for cod. The main reason is mackerel's higher fat content.

That does not make mackerel a worse choice. It is an oily fish and provides long-chain omega-3 fats. It simply ranks differently if the question changes from “which fish has the most protein?” to “which fish gives me the most protein for the fewest calories?”

3. Trout: around 23 grams per 100 g

The farmed rainbow trout entry provides about 23.8 g/100 g, while the wild rainbow trout entry is about 22.9 g/100 g.

That is a difference of less than 1 gram per 100 g. In a 5-ounce serving, the difference is only around 1.3 g of protein, so both are very similar protein sources in practice.

4. Swordfish: high in protein, with an important mercury consideration

Cooked swordfish provides about 23.5 g of protein and 172 calories per 100 g. A 5-ounce portion would provide roughly 33 g of protein.

FDA/EPA list swordfish among the fish with the highest mercury levels and classify it as a “Choice to Avoid” for people who are or may become pregnant, those who are breastfeeding, and children. That does not change its protein content, but it does change how useful the number is when deciding what to eat regularly.

5. Cod: less protein than tuna, but far fewer calories than mackerel

Cooked Atlantic cod provides about 22.8 g of protein and 105 calories per 100 g. Compared with the tuna in the table, that is about 6.4 g less protein per 100 g. Compared with mackerel, it is only about 1.1 g less protein but around 157 fewer calories.

That makes cod especially efficient when the goal is a lot of protein with relatively little energy. Salted cod is a different product because salting changes water content and raises sodium substantially.

6. Salmon: slightly less protein, a very different fat profile

Cooked farmed Atlantic salmon provides about 22.1 g of protein and 206 calories per 100 g. That is roughly 7.1 g less protein per 100 g than the tuna entry, but salmon contains much more fat.

That fat is part of salmon's nutritional value because salmon is a major source of EPA and DHA. Ranking below tuna for protein does not make it nutritionally inferior; it simply answers a different question.

What about canned sardines and anchovies?

Canned fish can also be very high in protein, but it is not directly equivalent to a cooked fresh fillet because water, sodium and sometimes oil are different.

As a rough reference, drained canned sardines can provide about 24–25 g of protein per 100 g, while drained oil-packed anchovies can approach 29 g/100 g. Anchovies are normally eaten in much smaller portions and contain far more sodium than a plain cooked fillet.

Canned sardines with edible bones also provide substantial calcium, which is another reason not to judge them only by protein.

Does raw fish have less protein?

Per 100 g, raw fish can show a somewhat lower protein concentration than the same fish after cooking because it contains more water. Cooking removes moisture and concentrates the remaining nutrients into less weight.

If a fillet loses about 20% of its weight mainly as water, the protein per 100 g can rise even though the total protein in that piece changes little. No new protein appears; the proportion of water changes.

For sushi or sashimi, use composition data for the specific raw fish. For a simple species comparison, it is clearer not to mix raw values into a cooked ranking.

White fish vs. oily fish: protein is often quite similar

In the table, cod provides 22.8 g/100 g and salmon 22.1 g/100 g, a difference of only about 0.7 g. Mackerel is somewhat higher at 23.9 g.

The bigger distinction is fat. Cod is very lean; salmon and mackerel contain much more fat and energy, while also providing more long-chain omega-3 fats.

Protein per serving

FishServingApprox. protein
Cooked tuna5 oz41 g
Cooked mackerel5 oz34 g
Cooked trout5 oz34 g
Cooked cod5 oz32 g
Cooked salmon5 oz31 g
Drained canned sardines3.5 oz24–25 g

At normal serving sizes, all of these fish provide substantial protein. The difference between a 5-ounce serving of cod and salmon is only about 1 gram of protein; the difference between salmon and tuna is closer to 10 grams.

So which fish should you choose?

If protein concentration is the only criterion, tuna ranks very high. If calories matter too, cod and other lean white fish are especially efficient. If omega-3 intake matters, salmon, mackerel and sardines offer a different advantage.

For adults, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend at least 8 ounces of seafood per week on a 2,000-calorie pattern. FDA/EPA recommend that people who are or might become pregnant or are breastfeeding eat 8–12 ounces per week from lower-mercury choices. Variety matters because fish differ not just in protein but also in fat, omega-3s and mercury.

Sources

Protein and calorie values are based on USDA FoodData Central. Mercury and serving guidance comes from the FDA/EPA Advice about Eating Fish.

faq.question: Which fish is highest in protein?
faq.answer: Among the cooked fish compared, yellowfin tuna provides about 29.2 g of protein per 100 g. Mackerel and trout are close to 24 g, while cod and salmon are around 22–23 g.

faq.question: Does salmon have less protein than tuna?
faq.answer: Yes in these references: cooked salmon provides about 22.1 g/100 g versus 29.2 g/100 g for cooked yellowfin tuna. Salmon contains much more fat and is a strong source of EPA and DHA omega-3s.

faq.question: Does white fish have less protein than oily fish?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Cooked cod provides about 22.8 g/100 g and cooked salmon about 22.1 g/100 g. The bigger difference is usually fat, not protein.

faq.question: Is canned fish high in protein?
faq.answer: Yes. Drained canned sardines can provide about 24–25 g/100 g and drained oil-packed anchovies close to 29 g/100 g, although canned products can contain much more sodium and, when packed in oil, more calories.
